source.title: Heart Disease Prediction: A Comparative Study of Optimisers Performance in Deep Neural Networks

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It has minor typographical and formatting issues, but no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: Compares optimizers on a natural-label clinical prediction task and reports training and validation losses plus classification metrics, using a different setting and measures from V4's source studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for ten optimizers. Rows cover the separately reported training/validation losses, stability values, and classification metrics; the final model's combined enhancement result is also recorded. Prior-work results in Related Works are not included.
record.test_reason: The study compares adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out performance in a new setting: tabular heart-disease classification. It bears on V4, although the initial comparison uses no hyperparameter tuning.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors select RMSprop for its balance of predictive metrics and convergence speed, acknowledge its limited stability, and report approximately 92% ROC-AUC after combined enhancements, compared with approximately 84% initially.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a six-hidden-layer fully connected network on a heart disease dataset, compares ten optimizers under a shared initialization, and reports validation loss and clinical classification metrics rather than the source version's image and language benchmark comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer choice changes convergence epoch, validation-loss stability, and reported precision, recall, and AUC. The paper reports the enhanced result with dropout, tuning, and early stopping together.

fits_no_version.finding: The enhanced RMSprop recipe raises reported ROC-AUC from approximately 84% to 92%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A combined change involving dropout, learning-rate tuning, early stopping and cross-validation improves reported performance on this clinical task; individual contributions are undetermined.

record.problems: One dataset and one fixed architecture; the authors note dataset size and structure and model architecture may have influenced results. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The enhanced ROC-AUC result combines dropout, hyperparameter tuning, and early stopping, so their individual contributions are not isolated. Table 2 reports identical losses for SGD and SGD Nesterov and for Adam and AdamW.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the reported optimizer tables. Results for convergence epoch and stability are not separately rowed because they do not directly measure the training-test generalization gap named by V4.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width variation beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and local connectivity.

Image and language benchmarks; learning-rate and decay-schedule tuning in the initial comparison; comparative broader tuning; controlled weight-decay recovery; switching optimizers; word-level language models.
Batch-size comparisons and adaptations under fixed epoch budgets.
The isolated effect of dropout, dependence on training-set size or dropout strength, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Table values match the supplied text. Tables 2 and 4 combine distinct performance measures that should be separated for verdicts. Table 4's evaluation partition is not explicitly identified. Initial optimizer hyperparameters and uncertainty across runs are not reported. A larger training-validation gap does not by itself establish worse held-out performance than SGD.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Network width beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Image-classification and language benchmarks; broader hyperparameter tuning; decoupled weight decay and optimizer switching; word-level language models.
Large-batch versus small-batch training, fixed epoch budgets, and recipe adaptations.
The effect of dropout cannot be separated from hyperparameter tuning and early stopping in the enhanced setup.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: SGD
rows.size_stated: six fully connected hidden layers; neuron sizes [16, 32, 64, 32, 16, 8]
rows.operation_detail: Trained the fixed DNN with SGD from the shared initialization.
rows.measure: Final training loss / final validation loss; precision; recall; AUC
rows.note: The training loss is lower than validation loss; SGD is the non-adaptive comparison for the optimizer results.
rows.check: Valid SGD comparator, but its training-validation gap alone cannot establish an adaptive-optimizer disadvantage. The subject is a DNN trained with SGD, rather than SGD itself.

rows.note: The text says adaptive optimizers such as Adam showed stronger overfitting than SGD.
rows.check: Adam has much worse validation loss despite lower training loss than SGD, but slightly higher AUC and higher recall. Split loss and classification metrics into separate rows; a training-validation gap alone is not the comparison V4 names.
